blocks.text: Market Update5

blocks.html: The second quarter brought some resolution to the two shocks that had defined Q1 and did so against the bears. Brent crude fell 31% over the quarter to $69.50/bbl, its steepest quarterly decline since the 2020 crash, as a 60-day US-Iran ceasefire reopened the Strait of Hormuz and drained the war premium that had driven crude to a $126 peak. The rate path moved in the opposite direction and with equal force: an 8-4 April FOMC vote, a hot 3.8% May CPI print, and Kevin Warsh's confirmation as Fed Chair repriced year-end expectations from three cuts at the start of the year to hike odds as high as 47%. Warsh's first meeting cemented the shift - rates were held unanimously, forward guidance was dropped, and the median dot moved to point at a 2026 hike rather than a cut. Despite the volatility, risk assets rallied hard. The S&P 500 rose 15%, its best quarter since 2020, powered by a Q1 earnings season that delivered roughly 25% EPS

blocks.html: Leveraged loans returned +1.89%6 in Q2 but closed the softest first half for the asset class in four years. The weakness was concentrated rather than broad with Software as the epicenter. The average bid on Software loans fell to a YTD low near $85 against roughly $97 for the rest of the market, a 12-point gap that marks the widest of the cycle, with software loans down more than 6% YTD. Quality bifurcation widened alongside it - single-B loans turned negative in June for the first time since February while BB rated loans stayed positive every month of the year and stressed/distressed paper climbed to 12.7% of the market from 8.8% at year-end. Primary activity reflected defense over offense: Q2 volume totaled $224 billion, down 7% QoQ, and shifted toward amendments, including a record $29.5 billion of amend-to-extend as sponsors chipped away at the 2028 maturity wall. Software's share of new-issue BSL volume collapsed to roughly 9% YTD from 17.6% in 2025 - the lowest since 2013 - with Healthcare leading issuance for the first time since 2015. The technical bid was thin throughout: true new CLO issuance fell to $33.3 billion, the slowest since Q4 2023, and investor demand of $34.5 billion ran at roughly half the typical 2024-25 pace. Defaults, by contrast, eased through the quarter - 1.34% in April, 1.35% in May, and 0.97% in June - as last year's large defaults rolled off the trailing window.

blocks.html: CLO liability spreads retraced through the second quarter, reversing from the March wides as risk appetite recovered following the post-crisis tights that opened the year. Issuance technicals were a partial driver of the spread movement. Second quarter volume totaled approximately $128 billion, with refinancing and reset activity accounting for approximately $95 billion, or 74%, versus approximately $33 billion, or 26%, of true new issuance — the highest refinancing and reset share of total issuance since the first quarter of 2017.

blocks.html: Spreads on AAA through BBB rated CLO tranches now stand flat to modestly tighter versus year-end 20257, as the second quarter rally more than offset the first quarter back-up. BB rated CLO debt was the exception, with new issue BB rated debt spreads remaining approximately 40 basis points wider than year-end levels (515 basis points versus 475 basis points)7, making BB tranches the one part of the capital structure where the rally has not fully reversed the earlier widening. Additionally, the Q2 rally that carried high yield corporate bond spreads back to its early-year tights has yet to reach CLO BB tranches. We view this disconnect as a reason for CLO BB spreads to tighten.

blocks.html: Fund trading in the second quarter captured two distinct opportunities. In April, new CLO issuance was still pricing at wide levels in the wake of the software sector selloff, so we purchased AAA through BBB rated paper at significantly wider levels just ahead of the broader market recovery. In May and June, we extended this trade to AA and A rated tranches by applying the same primary/secondary arbitrage strategy we have frequently employed in the Fund, which was historically concentrated in AAA rated paper. Outlook10

blocks.html: Investment grade CLO debt spreads staged a broad recovery over the second quarter, retracing the first- quarter back-up to stand flat to modestly tighter versus year-end 2025. In our view, encouragingly, a number of emerging tailwinds, discussed below, could help sustain and extend this tightening across the investment grade CLO capital stack in the months ahead.
blocks.text: Investment grade CLO debt spreads staged a broad recovery over the second quarter, retracing the first- quarter back-up to stand flat to modestly tighter versus year-end 2025. In our view, encouragingly, a number of emerging tailwinds, discussed below, could help sustain and extend this tightening across the investment grade CLO capital stack in the months ahead.

items: The first of these tailwinds is the elevated, and potentially still-rising, base rate environment. Persistently high base rates — with the market now pricing in some probability of further hikes — continue to favor floating-rate products like floating rate CLO debt, driving incremental demand and higher all-in yields; we believe this is already evident in CLO ETF flows, with JAAA, the largest CLO AAA-rated exchange-traded fund, receiving over $1 billion of inflows in June alone.11 As this demand builds across the capital structure, we believe it should help compress spreads across the capital stack. In our view, current investors in the Fund also stand to benefit directly, as the Fund's current coupon yield would rise correspondingly in a rising rate environment, all else equal.

items: As discussed above, the second tailwind — worth revisiting given its direct relevance to the Fund's investment grade mandate — relates to ongoing shifts in the regulatory capital treatment of insurer holdings of CLO debt on both sides of the Atlantic. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners' (NAIC) risk-based capital regime in the US and the Solvency II framework in Europe require insurers to hold capital against balance sheet assets in proportion to each asset's perceived risk, with higher capital charges reducing the effective return on holding that asset.13 As we highlighted, the revised NAIC framework would result in significant reductions in capital charges for AAA through single-A tranches. On the European side, the European Commission's Solvency II recalibration — formally adopted in October 2025 and published in the EU Official Journal in February 2026 — materially lowers the spread-risk capital charges insurers must hold against AAA-rated CLO tranches, with the new charges set to apply from January 30, 2027. Together, we believe these reforms should support incremental insurer demand across the investment grade capital structure over time. We believe the picture is more nuanced for BBB tranches as the NAIC treatment is more sensitive to a tranche's credit enhancement, so thinner BBB tranches with less structural protection could see more muted relief — or even a modest increase — in capital charges.

Weaker new-issue economics have already begun to weigh on activity: Year to date through June 30, 2026, broadly syndicated loan new issue CLO volumes are down 23% versus the same period in 2025.14 We expect this slowdown in new issue CLO volumes to reduce the supply of new AAA through BBB rated CLO paper coming to market, tightening the technical backdrop for outstanding investment grade tranches and supporting AAA through BBB spread compression over time.

items: In our opinion, one near-term technical headwind bears monitoring: approximately 28% of outstanding AAA CLO paper will be callable by year-end 2026 with coupons at or above 130 basis points15, well above current new-issue clearing levels, which stand in the low 120 basis point range. As these transactions exit their non-call periods, collateral managers face a clear economic incentive to refinance or reset, and we expect the resulting pipeline of AAA supply to continue pressuring senior spreads in the near term, which could delay — though not derail — broader tightening across the Fund's AAA through BBB rated tranches. Importantly, we view this pressure as a temporary technical dynamic rather than a lasting shift, as refinancing and reset activity does not introduce net new supply to the market; any associated spread widening should recede as the pipeline is absorbed, clearing the way for continued CLO AAA through BBB spread tightening. In our view, any such temporary widening would also set up an attractive backdrop to continue the primary/secondary arbitrage strategy discussed above, allowing the Fund to add AAA and other investment grade tranches at wider levels ahead of the eventual retracement — consistent with the opportunistic purchases the Fund made in April following the software sector selloff.16
